title: A Life in Four Stages
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: Butterflies are among the most familiar insects, and there are about eighteen thousand species, found on every continent except Antarctica. They range in size from the tiny western pygmy blue, which measures about one centimetre across its wings, to the Queen Alexandra's birdwing of Papua New Guinea, whose wings can span about a quarter of a metre. Though fragile in appearance, butterflies are remarkable survivors, and their life cycle, which has four separate stages, is one of the most striking transformations in nature.

The cycle begins with an egg. A female butterfly lays her eggs, often hundreds in a lifetime, on a particular kind of plant, which she recognises by taste, using sensors on her feet. The choice is important, because the young that hatch will feed on this plant, and the wrong one would starve them. The eggs are tiny, usually smaller than a pinhead, and may be round, oval or shaped like a barrel. They hatch in three to ten days, depending on the temperature.

From the egg comes the larva, which is called a caterpillar. Its only job is to eat, and it does so almost without stopping, increasing its weight by about a thousand times in only two weeks. Because its skin cannot stretch, the caterpillar must shed it several times as it grows, a process known as moulting. Many caterpillars have bright colours or spines to warn birds that they taste bad, while others look like twigs or bird droppings, so that predators ignore them.

When it has grown as large as it can, the caterpillar attaches itself to a twig or a leaf and changes into a pupa, called a chrysalis. From outside, it seems that nothing is happening. Inside, however, the body of the caterpillar breaks down almost completely, and a new body, with wings, legs and eyes, is built from the remains. Some pupae are camouflaged to look like dead leaves, and others are decorated with spots of shining gold. This stage lasts about two weeks, but in cold climates it may last all winter.

The adult butterfly breaks out of the chrysalis, and at first its wings are wet and folded. It hangs still for several hours, pumping fluid into the wings to open them and waiting for them to dry. Then it flies away to find food and a mate. Adults drink nectar through a long tube called a proboscis, which is rolled up when not in use, and they help plants by carrying pollen from flower to flower. Most live for only a few weeks, though some species survive for ten months. Males and females often look quite different from each other, and in some species the males gather in groups beside puddles to drink the minerals dissolved in the water.

A few butterflies make extraordinary journeys. The monarch butterfly of North America flies up to four thousand kilometres to spend the winter in the mountain forests of central Mexico. No single butterfly makes the return trip: it takes several generations to travel back north in spring. How the young find the way to a place that they have never seen remains a mystery, although scientists believe that they use the position of the Sun and the Earth's magnetic field.

Butterflies are now in danger in many countries. The destruction of meadows and forests, the use of chemicals on farms, and the warming of the climate have all reduced their numbers. In some regions, the numbers have fallen by half in only a few decades. Dr Tomas Brandt, a butterfly specialist, says that butterflies are an early warning of damage to the environment, since they respond quickly to change. He recommends that gardeners plant native flowers and leave some areas of grass uncut.
